street_king.title: Street King
epilogue: A year later. You sit in the plastic chair at the motor park office. It still has Baba Ticket's shape in it.

epilogue.text: Baba Ticket now sells suya two streets away. He gives you extra pepper. You are never sure it is a kindness.
Baba Ticket retired to his third wife's house in Ìkòròdú. He calls every Friday to quote a proverb wrong.

epilogue: Every morning the drivers line up and pay. Some pay because they respect you. Some pay because they remember Scatter's glasses in the puddle.

epilogue.text: The co-op board still stands beside Ada's Corner. Three o's. You never let anybody fix it.

epilogue: At 5:40 a.m. a boy steps off the night bus with a phone on 3% battery. Somebody who is definitely not a conductor walks towards him.
You stand up. "Oya. Come here, JJC."

cult_boss.title: Cult Boss
epilogue: The curtain at the Shell House opens for the first time in twenty years.
Behind it: a desk, a stamp, a very old man in a brown cardigan, and nine thousand files.
"Number One Shell," he says, and slides the stamp across the desk. "You cannot refuse. Nobody ever could. That is why nobody asks."

epilogue.text: Ada does not come to the ceremony. She sends a note: "Ask for the receipt."
Somewhere in the files there is one with Sunday's name on it. You never open it. You never throw it away either.

epilogue: You sit. The chair is warm. Outside, the Hyenas are quiet, and the junction pays its dues on time.
Your first official act is to sign Form T-12 for a nervous boy with a phone on 3% battery. Nine pages. In triplicate.

wanted.title: Wanted
epilogue: Night. The back of Formula One's okada. No helmet, no plan, one bag.
"Where we dey go?" he shouts over the engine.
"Anywhere wey road go."
Behind you, Iyana-Wahala's lights shrink to one orange dot under the flyover. A green van sits at the junction with its siren off.

epilogue.text: Bassey is in the van. He watches you go. He does not radio anybody. Not tonight.
Your phone buzzes. Iya Bọ́sẹ̀. You let it ring all the way to Ogun State.

epilogue: Formula One laughs into the wind. For the first time since you arrived, so do you.

legit_businessman.title: Legit Businessman

epilogue.text: Iyana-Wahala Transport Ltd. Three yellow danfos. A real office with a real receipt book.
Iyana-Wahala Transport Ltd, owned by the Okafor family. Three yellow danfos. Ada does the accounts. Nobody argues with the accounts.
Ada is your business partner. Her first rule: no fee without receipt. Her second rule: no receipt without fee.

epilogue: The first danfo is called "Rule Number One". Bíọ́dún drives it, singing.

epilogue.text: Sunday is the conductor. He dances at every stop. Passengers tip him to stop dancing. He takes the money and dances more.

epilogue: Your drivers pay one fair fee to one co-operative and nobody else.
Some mornings you still wake up at 5:40, ready to run.

informant.title: The Informant
epilogue: Abuja. A two-bedroom flat with air conditioning, a guard, and nothing to do.
Your new name is Emmanuel. You keep forgetting it.

epilogue.text: On TV, Barrister Settlement leaves a courthouse with his face covered by a very expensive file folder.
On TV, the Shell House is sealed with yellow tape. Somebody has stamped the tape. Twice.

epilogue: The food here is fine. It is just... fine. You would sell your new name for one plate of Mama Put's ewa agoyin.
At night you call out bus stops in your sleep. The guard has started answering.

rock_bottom.title: Rock Bottom

epilogue.text: You wake up in a ward at General Hospital Iyana-Wahala. Nurse Rónkẹ́ is counting drips like money.
The election ends. The posters peel. You are standing at the Back Side with nothing: no crew, no co-op, no shell, no savings.

epilogue: "You again," says Nurse Rónkẹ́, and then, softer: "Eat something."
Your phone rings. It's Mama. You don't have the strength to lie any more.
"{name}, come home. We go find the money together. Market women no dey kill person. Dem just dey talk until you wish dem kill you."
You laugh. It hurts. You laugh anyway.

jailed.title: Jailed
epilogue: Awaiting Trial. Cell 4. Forty men, one window, one bucket.

epilogue.text: A man in the corner holds up a hand with three fingers. "Ah," says Professor. "Rule number thirteen: never get caught. I forgot to teach you that one."
An old man in the corner squints at you. "Iyana-Wahala? Jimoh Professor's boy? Sit down. I was his cellmate in '98. Let me teach you the rules of the cell."
Every Sunday, Ada brings moi-moi and the accounts. Every Sunday she says, "Next month."

epilogue: Your case file is on a desk somewhere, under nine other case files.
Outside, somebody else is calling your stop.

go_home.title: Go Home
epilogue: The last alert goes through at 9:14 a.m. ₦0 owing.
In Ìlú-Àlàáfíà, Iya Bọ́sẹ̀ reads the message twice, puts down her phone, and declares a market holiday nobody asked for.
You go home in Bíọ́dún's danfo. "God's Time Is The Best" is full of gifts: rice, a generator, a framed photo of the Iyana-Wahala co-op board, three o's.
Mama is standing at the junction when you arrive. She looks at you for a long time. Then she slaps your arm, hard, and doesn't let go of it.

epilogue.text: Ada comes too. Mama inspects her like a goat at market, then gives her the best chair.
Professor sends a voice note: "Rule number one hundred: go home while home is still there. Well done, my son."

epilogue: That night the whole town eats. Nobody mentions Double-Double. Everybody mentions it the next morning.

the_honourable.title: The Honourable
epilogue: Councillor {name}, Iyana-Wahala Ward. Independent. Elected by a margin nobody could rig because everybody was watching.
Hon. Mrs. Ronke Ademola-Peters sends flowers. Hon. Owó Ńlá sends a lawyer. Barrister Settlement sends his congratulations, and his card, in case.
Your first act in office is a community feeding programme.
The rice bags arrive on Monday. Your face is printed on every one of them.
You stare at the bags for a long time.
Then you sign for them.
The cycle continues.

_fates.text: Professor: buried under the flyover's shadow. On his grave someone painted Rule Number One.
Professor: serving the time that should have been yours. He runs the prison canteen. Badly.
Professor: Professor's Kitchen, beside Mama Put. The rules are on the wall. Rule number one is still spelled wrong.
Professor: teaching goats the rules of the road in his sister's village.
Professor: same corner, same chair, watching the Back Side.
Ada: together with you, when you're honest. Saving for university. Still laughing at your lies.
Ada: your best friend. Her shop has a second container now.
Ada: she got into university. She didn't tell you. You heard from Mallam Garba.
Sunday: out of the Hyenas. Still dancing at every stop.
Sunday: still a Hyena on paper. Still your friend in secret.
Sunday: gone. Some nights you hear a conductor laugh and you turn around.
Scatter: runs Under-Bridge "with your permission". He is still 5'4". He still asks you not to mention it.
Scatter: still waiting for his turn. Lagos is round.
Mama's debt: paid in full. Iya Bọ́sẹ̀ has found someone new to send voice notes to.
Mama's debt: {debt} still owing. The voice notes continue.

grace_grace.title: Grass to Grace
epilogue: A year later. A spare-parts shop in Nkwọ-Agụụ junction, the first one between here and the city. Honest parts. The sign says EMEKA & SONS, though there are no sons yet.

epilogue.text: There are no sons yet. Chinwe says to be patient. Chinwe says a lot of things. You listen to all of them.
On market days, Ọnyịsị buys his bicycle chain from you and tells the story of the thief who confessed under the tree. He improves it every time.
Nne sits outside the shop in the afternoons and tells customers what you did in Lagos. All of it. She is proud of the coming back, not the going.

epilogue: It is not much money. It is yours.
Grace, it turns out, is not the opposite of grass. It's what grows on it when you stop burning the field.

grace_unbound.title: Unbound
epilogue: The page burns blue, then white, then nothing. Thirty miles away in Zone 5, a white book closes by itself.
Chief Ọ̀dụ̀ stands very still in the firelight. For the first time anybody can remember, he looks old.

epilogue.text: Papa's name rises out of the fire as smoke. The old men say they saw his face in it. The old men say a lot of things on festival nights.
The next morning Nne calls you from the kitchen. By your name. Twice. Just to hear it.
Chinwe looks at you at the festival and frowns, as if remembering a dream. A week later she knocks on your door. 'I think I know you,' she says. 'Tell me how.'

epilogue: The money goes with the page. All of it. The Benz won't start. The house in Zone 5 belongs to someone else's cousin now.
You are poor, and free, and the drums are very loud.

grace_witness.title: The Witness
epilogue: Federal High Court, Lagos. Day forty of the trial. You are in the witness box for the ninth time.
Chief Ọ̀dụ̀ sits in the dock in a grey suit. He looks smaller without the white.

epilogue.text: You go to prison too: eighteen months, reduced for cooperation. Commander Bassey visits on Sundays and brings akara. He says it's for the case. It's not for the case.
You walk out of court each evening a free man with a police escort and a very long memory.

epilogue: The white book is Exhibit 14. It sits in a glass case. Nobody in the courtroom will look at it for long.

epilogue.text: Ike testifies by video from a country with good weather. At the end, for the first time in years, he laughs. The judge has to call for order.

grace_goldenCage.title: Golden Cage
epilogue: Zone 5. A gate that opens by itself. A garden with lights in the trees. A house too big to have a sound in it.
You have everything. You count it every night. It doesn't like to be counted. You count it anyway.

epilogue.text: Nne calls on Sundays. She says 'my son' and 'my child' and 'you'. She never says your name. You never ask her to.
You have covered every mirror in the house with white cloth. It seemed like the right colour.
Sometimes you think you see Ike at the gate. It's always the gardener.

epilogue: Outside, Lagos laughs at something. The sound doesn't reach the house.

grace_whiteCloth.title: The White Cloth
epilogue: The cloth is soft. Softer than anything you have ever worn. It fits as if it was cut for you years ago.
You ride back to Lagos in the third white car. Behind you, the festival fire gets smaller, then it's a star, then it's gone.
A year later you sit in the white room. A boy from a village you've never heard of sits in the white chair. His eyes are hungry.
You ask him who he loves most in the world.
You don't laugh. You can't remember when you stopped.

grace_prodigal.title: The Prodigal
epilogue: You stay. You have nothing. You have the morning.

epilogue.text: Nne makes you pepper soup and doesn't ask any questions. She doesn't need to. She watches you eat like you are still nine years old.
Nne lets you sleep in the parlour. She is polite to you, which is the worst thing a mother can be.
You owe the village {villageDebt}. You go back to the quarry. Every stone is a naira. It will take years. You start anyway.
At Chinwe's wedding you dance at the back, badly, and nobody minds.

epilogue: On the third morning, Dibia Ọ̀kwụ̀ walks past your door and nods. Not approval. Recognition. That's enough to start with.

_fates_grace.text: Papa's land: still the family's. Yams grow there. Papa would have complained about how they're planted.
Papa's land: fenced, sold, someone else's. Nne walks the long way round it to the stream.
The school roof: finished. The children don't know whose money it was. That's how it should be.
The school roof: still leaking. When it rains, the children move their benches and keep reading.
Ike: far away, still running, almost laughing.
Ike: nobody knows. You know. You don't say.
Ike: taken by the white cars. His mother still sets a plate for him on Sundays.
Chinwe: your wife. She keeps the accounts and your secrets, in that order.
Chinwe: she chose you, in front of her whole family. Her father hasn't forgiven either of you. He's coming round.
The driver with the failed brakes: he still tells passengers about the JJC who sold him fake parts. He doesn't know your name. He describes your face very accurately.
The driver with the failed brakes: you paid for his repairs. He brings you his customers now.
The village: it believed you about Ike, mostly. Some of the elders still look at you a second too long.
The white book: you never read it. Some nights you wonder what your page said.
Nne: she still says 'ask yourself if you'll tell me at Christmas'. You still do.
The gate in Zone 5: you never went near it again. You still run, in dreams.
Commander Bassey: he kept your file. He keeps everybody's file. Yours has a note in the margin: 'village boy. watch.'
The money: you gave some of it away. It's the only part you remember spending.
Dibia Ọ̀kwụ̀: still peeling oranges by the stream. Still right about most things.
Nne: you told her everything was fine. She let you believe she believed it.
The white envelope: you burned it. Some nights you still smell gold ink.
The white chair: you ran from it. It is still waiting, they say, in a house with no number.
